## R Markdown

```{r}
    getwd()
rawData <- read.csv('./dataset/heart.csv',header=T)
head(rawData)

```

```{r}
# Look for any missing or weird values and see how many unique values each column has
sapply(rawData,function(x) sum(is.na(x))) 
sapply(rawData,function(x) length(unique(x))) 
```

```{r}
# We know there are no missing values, but we are going to visualize just to be sure 
missmap(rawData, main="Missing values")

# Observed = 100% which is great because that means there are no missing values. But we will have to look for non-physiological (values that don't make sense clinically).

# Looking at the unique values, they tend to make sense. Chol and thalach both have a lot of unique values, but this makes sense considering that both cholestorol levels and heart rate can vary significantly

```

```{r}
# Since our data set has clinical data, there may be data here that is not physiologically possible.
summary(rawData)

# Some variables have extreme numbers, but are still physically possible to achieve We don' have any unusually low numbers, so we do not have to won't about that. The column that sticks out is ca (number of major vessels (0-3) colored by flourosopy). We can see that the max is 4, but this column is only supposed to contain the numbers 0-3.

# Since we want to keep this data, we will have to replace it. Since it is a non-numeric value, we will replace it with the most frequently occurring value.
mostFreqOccur <- rawData %>% count(ca)
print(mostFreqOccur)

# The most common number if 0, so we will impute the values that have 4 with the value 0.
# Easiest way to make the values na and replace the na values with 0. We will just keep tham as na until we split the raw dat into testing and training sets

rawData$ca[rawData$ca == 4] <- NA

```

```{r}

# Next, we will look for any possible outliers
summary(rawData)

# Chol might have outliers.
boxplot(rawData$chol)

# We have a few outliers chol above ~ 350. There are about 26 total outiers.
cho350 <- rawData %>% 
                filter(chol > 350) %>% 
                select(chol)

# We will deal with the outliers by using the log function
summary(log(rawData$chol)) # Smaller range, so there should be no skew

heart_disease <- rawData
heart_disease$chol <- log(heart_disease$chol)

# See the new data frame with updated values
head(heart_disease)

```

```{r}
# We need to treat the categorical variables as factor. As mentioned before, all of the data is encoded numerically, meaning that our categorical variables are represented by numbers.

# Categorical variables: sex, cp, fbs restecg, exang, slope, ca, thal
heart_disease$sex<- as.factor(heart_disease$sex)
heart_disease$cp <- as.factor(heart_disease$cp)
heart_disease$fbs<- as.factor(heart_disease$fbs)
heart_disease$restecg <- as.factor(heart_disease$restecg)
heart_disease$exang <- as.factor(heart_disease$exang)
heart_disease$slope <- as.factor(heart_disease$slope)
heart_disease$ca <- as.factor(heart_disease$ca)
heart_disease$thal<- as.factor(heart_disease$thal)

head(heart_disease) # Make sure the headers of the categorical variables are now factors
```

```{r}
# Splitting the raw data into training and testing set. ~ 80% of out data will be used for the training, and ~ 20% will be used for testing

intrain <- createDataPartition(y = heart_disease$target, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)

hd_training <- heart_disease[intrain,] #Create training set
hd_testing <- heart_disease[-intrain,] #Create testing

# Now we will impute 0 for the rows that have 4 in ca
hd_training$ca[is.na(hd_training$ca)] <- 0
hd_testing$ca[is.na(hd_testing$ca)] <- 0
```

```{r}
# Export cleaned data frame
write.csv(heart_disease, "heart_disease_cleaned.csv", row.names = FALSE)

#Export training and testing
write.csv(hd_training, "heart_disease_train.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(hd_testing, "heart_disease_test.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
save(hd_training, hd_testing, file = "heart_disease_split.RData")
save(heart_disease, file = "heart_disease_cleaned.RData")

```

```{r}
# Simple chart of the proportions: this chart is the foundation of the data, it being balanced is a good thing. 
barplot(
  table(heart_disease$target),
  col = c("green4", "red3"),
  names.arg = c("No Heart Disease", "Heart Disease"),
  main = "Distribution of Heart Disease Outcome",
  ylab = "Count"
)

```
